quantization_breakthroughs.analysis: By mid-2026 the practical frontier for fitting large models into small VRAM has shifted from naive 4-bit to a family of activation- and error-aware schemes. The mainstream trio remains GGUF (llama.cpp's k-quants and the newer i-quants like IQ2_XXS/IQ3 plus the imatrix calibration), GPTQ, and AWQ, but the bar for quality at low bit-width has moved sharply. AWQ protects the most salient activation channels and now delivers near-lossless Q4 on 30-70B models; GPTQ's one-shot layerwise error minimization pairs with Marlin/ExLlama kernels for high throughput; and GGUF Q4_K_M/Q5_K_M is the default for mixed CPU/GPU and Apple Silicon. Rough memory math drives the story: a 30B model is ~60GB at FP16, ~15GB at INT8, and ~7.5GB of raw weights at 4-bit, so a 4060 Ti 16GB or even an 8-12GB card can hold a Q4 30B-class model's weights, with the remaining budget going to KV cache and context.
quantization_breakthroughs.details: The research/exotic tier — AQLM (additive quantization, ~2-bit), QuIP# (incoherence processing + lattice codebooks), and HQQ (fast, calibration-free half-quadratic quantization) — pushes toward 2-2.5 bits, where AQLM and QuIP# can keep a 70B model usable on a single 24GB card and a 30B model comfortably under 12GB. The headline quality metric is perplexity delta: well-tuned Q4 (AWQ/GPTQ/GGUF k-quant) typically costs <1 point of perplexity and retains ~98%+ of original task quality, while 2-bit AQLM/QuIP# trade a few points of perplexity for a further ~2x weight shrink. The practical enabler for 30B+ on 8-16GB is the combination of (1) sub-4-bit weights, (2) imatrix/activation-aware calibration that concentrates precision where it matters, and (3) GPU kernels (Marlin, ExLlamaV2, llama.cpp i-quant kernels) that make these formats fast rather than merely small. For MoE models the effective active-parameter count matters more than total size, which compounds with quantization to put '30B-total' models squarely on budget hardware.

inference_engine_updates.analysis: The inference-engine field has bifurcated into datacenter throughput engines and consumer/edge engines, with steady convergence on the same core tricks. On NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell, TensorRT-LLM still holds the raw-throughput crown (Llama-3 70B on a single H100 can exceed ~900-1200 tok/s per request at batch 16+, and >15k tok/s aggregate in distributed setups), but vLLM (PagedAttention) and SGLang (RadixAttention prefix-cache reuse) have closed most of the gap and are far easier to deploy, routinely hitting 700-1200 tok/s/user on 70B-class models while excelling at many-request continuous batching. SGLang's RadixAttention specifically wins multi-user and agentic workloads where prompt prefixes repeat.
inference_engine_updates.details: On the consumer side, llama.cpp remains the universal baseline — CPU + partial GPU offload, GGUF, Metal/CUDA/ROCm/Vulkan backends, and the new MoE CPU-offload flags — delivering tens of tok/s for 13-30B-class models on a single mid-range GPU and 150-200+ tok/s for 7B-class models on Apple M3/M4. ExLlamaV2 is the speed leader for quantized (EXL2) weights on 3090/4090-class cards, frequently beating general-purpose engines at mid-low precision thanks to tightly tuned kernels and a flexible bit-rate format. KTransformers is the standout for heterogeneous CPU/GPU MoE serving, letting users keep attention/router on GPU while streaming expert FFNs from CPU/RAM, which is what makes giant MoE (DeepSeek-class) runnable on a single consumer GPU. PowerInfer targets on-device/sparse activation, exploiting 'hot' vs 'cold' neurons to reach usable speeds on phones and low-power hosts. Across all engines the shared optimizations are continuous batching, paged/quantized KV cache, FlashAttention-class kernels, CUDA graphs, and speculative decoding.

moe_offloading.analysis: MoE expert offloading is the single biggest 2025-2026 unlock for budget hardware, because MoE models activate only a small fraction of their weights per token. llama.cpp added the '--n-cpu-moe N' flag (and the related '--override-tensor'/'-ot' regex placement) that keeps the expert FFN tensors of N layers in CPU/RAM while the attention, router, and shared/dense layers stay on the GPU. Since only a handful of experts fire per token, the hot path that actually runs each step is small, so a model with hundreds of billions of total parameters can be served with GPU VRAM sized to the active experts plus KV cache, spilling the cold expert weights to system RAM (or NVMe). This heterogeneous placement is what lets enthusiasts run DeepSeek-V3/R1-class and Qwen3-235B-A22B MoE on a single 16-24GB GPU paired with 64-128GB RAM.
moe_offloading.details: The practical recipe: push as many non-expert (attention + router + shared) layers onto the GPU as VRAM allows with -ngl, then use --n-cpu-moe to move expert tensors to CPU, tuning N up until it fits and down for speed. Tools like KTransformers formalize this with GPU-resident attention/KV and CPU-resident experts using AMX/AVX512 kernels, reporting large speedups over naive offload. The models this newly enables on budget rigs: Qwen3-30B-A3B (only ~3.3B active — trivially fast even with partial offload), Qwen3-235B-A22B (runnable on 16-24GB GPU + plenty of RAM), DeepSeek-V2/V3/R1 MoE, Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B, and GPT-OSS-class MoE. The key constraints become system RAM capacity and memory bandwidth rather than VRAM, and fast dual-channel/quad-channel DDR5 plus NVMe materially improve tok/s on offload-heavy runs.

budget_gpu_benchmarks.analysis: On budget GPUs the dominant lesson of 2025-2026 is that VRAM capacity, not raw compute, sets the ceiling — and that MoE plus offloading reshuffles what 'fits.' For dense models, an RTX 4060 Ti 16GB comfortably runs 14-20B-class 4-bit models fully in VRAM: measured ~22 tok/s on a 14B Q4 at 16K context and ~31 tok/s on a 20B (MXFP4) at long context, with prompt processing in the high hundreds of tok/s. A dense 30B at 4-bit (~18-22GB with context) does not fit fully in 16GB and falls off a cliff (single-digit tok/s) once it spills to system RAM. The RTX 3060 12GB is best for 7-13B 4-bit dense models (~15-22 tok/s on 7-8B Q4) and cannot hold a dense 30B.
budget_gpu_benchmarks.details: The game-changer for budget cards is MoE: because Qwen3-30B-A3B activates only ~3.3B parameters per token, a 4060 Ti 16GB (and even a 3060 12GB with some CPU offload) can run a '30B' MoE at very usable speeds — often 20-40+ tok/s — even though a dense 30B would be impractical on the same card. Practical configs: use Q4_K_M/Q5_K_M GGUF, push max -ngl that fits, reserve VRAM headroom for KV cache (quantize KV to Q8/Q4 for long context), and for large MoE add --n-cpu-moe to overflow cold experts to RAM. Older 24GB cards (3090) remain the value sweet spot for dense 30-34B fully on-GPU, while 12-16GB budget cards now punch far above their weight specifically by choosing MoE and quantized-KV configurations.

efficient_model_architectures.analysis: The clearest architectural win for quality-per-VRAM-GB is fine-grained MoE with a small active-parameter fraction, exemplified by Qwen3-30B-A3B: ~30.5B total parameters but only ~3.3B active per token, 128 experts with 8 activated, 60 layers, Grouped-Query Attention (96 query / 8 KV heads), and a native 32K context extendable to 128K-256K. This design stores 30B-scale knowledge while running with the latency and VRAM footprint closer to a 3-4B dense model, and benchmarks show it outperforming the dense QwQ-32B on several reasoning/code tasks despite roughly 10x fewer active parameters. The larger Qwen3-235B-A22B applies the same idea at scale (22B active of 235B total).
efficient_model_architectures.details: Beyond MoE, the best quality-per-GB comes from three converging trends: (1) GQA/MQA attention to shrink KV cache (the real long-context memory cost), (2) distillation, where strong small dense students (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 7B/14B/32B, Gemma/Phi-class) capture much of a larger teacher's capability in a 7-14B footprint, and (3) sparse/fine-grained experts with global load balancing that improve compute efficiency without quality loss. For a fixed VRAM budget the rough ranking is: small-active MoE (best knowledge-per-active-FLOP, but needs RAM for cold experts) > a well-distilled dense model of the size you can fully fit on GPU > a heavily quantized larger dense model. Practically, Qwen3-30B-A3B and similar 'A3B/A22B' MoE checkpoints, plus 7-14B distilled reasoners, give the best usable quality on 8-16GB cards in 2026.

memory_optimization.analysis: For long-context inference the KV cache, not the weights, becomes the dominant memory consumer, so the biggest 2025-2026 wins target it directly. PagedAttention (vLLM) eliminates KV fragmentation by allocating cache in fixed-size pages like OS virtual memory, raising effective batch size and concurrency; SGLang's RadixAttention reuses shared prompt prefixes across requests to avoid duplicate KV. On top of paging, KV-cache quantization (INT8/INT4, e.g., KVQuant-style and llama.cpp's --cache-type-k/v q8_0/q4_0) typically halves to quarters KV memory with minimal quality loss, directly extending the context that fits on a budget card. GQA/MQA architectures further shrink KV at the model level by sharing KV heads.
memory_optimization.details: FlashAttention (v2/v3) reduces attention's memory-bandwidth and avoids materializing the full attention matrix, with FA-3 adding Hopper-specific async and FP8 paths for faster, lower-memory long-context attention; these kernels are now standard in vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and increasingly llama.cpp. Speculative decoding (a small draft model proposing tokens verified in parallel by the target model, plus variants like Medusa/EAGLE/n-gram) cuts latency 2-3x without increasing the resident memory of the target model meaningfully. Ranked by memory-footprint impact for long context: (1) KV-cache quantization + GQA reduce the largest growing cost, (2) PagedAttention removes fragmentation waste and enables higher utilization, (3) FlashAttention removes the quadratic intermediate buffers, and (4) speculative decoding mainly buys speed rather than memory. Combined, these let multi-10K-to-100K-token contexts run on consumer GPUs that previously OOM'd.

community_discoveries.analysis: The r/LocalLLaMA community's consensus in 2025-2026 crystallized around three moves: pick a small-active MoE, quantize aggressively (Q4_K_M as the default, IQ-quants for the tightest fits), and use expert/KV offload to overflow what doesn't fit. The most-repeated finding is that MoE plus llama.cpp's --n-cpu-moe / -ot tensor-placement lets people run models far larger than their VRAM 'should' allow — e.g., Qwen3-235B-A22B and DeepSeek-V3/R1 on a single 16-24GB GPU backed by 64-128GB RAM — by keeping attention and router on GPU and streaming cold experts from system RAM. For pure-VRAM setups, Qwen3-30B-A3B at Q4 is the runaway recommendation for 8-16GB cards because its ~3.3B active parameters keep it fast even when partially offloaded.
community_discoveries.details: Concrete community configs that recur: set -ngl as high as fits, add --n-cpu-moe N (raise N until it loads, lower for speed), quantize KV with --cache-type-k/v q8_0 (or q4) to reclaim VRAM for context, and pin threads to physical cores for the CPU-resident experts. Tools like Ollama and LM Studio auto-tune much of this, while power users prefer raw llama.cpp/ExLlamaV2 for control. Real-world reports: ~50-60 tok/s for 8-9B Q4 fully on an 8GB card at 32K context; usable double-digit tok/s for 30B-A3B-class MoE on 12-16GB; and large MoE running at single-to-low-double-digit tok/s when heavily RAM-offloaded but stable thanks to improved memory-mapping. The community also stresses that fast DDR5 and NVMe meaningfully raise offload throughput, and that recurring 'offloading megathreads' track new flags and model-specific -ot regexes monthly.
